title: Unlearning That Lasts: Utility-Preserving, Robust, and Almost Irreversible Forgetting in LLMs
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Our method gives the best forgetting-utility trade-off, and stricter worst-case evaluation shows standard evaluation overstates how well other methods work.
layout: 2 panels, left scatter and right grouped bars, shared legend on top
description: A shared legend runs across the top and maps colors and markers to methods: Original (gray star), GradAscent (green), DPO (purple), NPO (gray), GradDiff (yellow), RMU (blue) and JensUn (ours, red diamond). The left panel is a scatter plot titled 'Improved unlearning (LPF)'. Its x-axis is response quality and its y-axis is forget-set accuracy. An orange-shaded 'Ideal zone' sits in the bottom right, and the red JensUn diamond lies inside it. The right panel is a grouped bar chart titled 'Enhanced unlearning evaluation (RWKU)'. Each method has a pair of bars, a plain bar for standard evaluation and a hatched bar for worst-case evaluation (ours). The hatched bars are consistently taller, for example 40 vs 68 for GradAscent. JensUn stays lowest, at 0 vs 6. A dashed vertical line separates the original LLM from the unlearned methods.
caption: Our JensUn yields the best trade-off between unlearning quality (forget set accuracy) and utility of the LLM. (left) Our unlearning method JensUn achieves on our LPF dataset an optimal worst-case forget set accuracy of 0% while maintaining high response quality (win rate of the unlearned vs the original model on AlpacaEval, see Section 4.3), the most similar to the original Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct pre-trained model. (right) Our novel worst-case evaluation using 9 paraphrases of the query on RWKU reveals that using single question-answer evaluations overestimates unlearning quality: our worst-case evaluation drastically increases forget set accuracy for the fine-tuned LLMs across different unlearning methods as well as the original model (Phi-3 Mini-4K-Instruct (3.8B)). The code and the associated LPF dataset can be found at https://github.com/nmndeep/JensU n-Unlearning.
abstract: Unlearning in large language models (LLMs) requires precisely removing specific information from a pre-trained model, e.g. to delete private data or harmful knowledge acquired during pre-training. However, existing unlearning methods often fall short under thorough evaluation. This paper makes three contributions. First, we introduce JensUn, a novel unlearning approach which leverages the Jensen-Shannon Divergence (JSD) as the training objective for both forget and retain sets. We provide theoretical arguments why JSD outperforms KL-Divergence, and show in extensive experiments that JensUn achieves the best forget-utility trade-off and demonstrates strong resilience to benign relearning, outperforming existing methods. Second, for a precise unlearning evaluation, we introduce LPF, a curated dataset of less prominent facts that provides a realistic unlearning scenario. Third, to comprehensively test unlearning methods, we $\textit{(i)}$ employ an LLM as semantic judge instead of the standard ROUGE score, and $\textit{(ii)}$ evaluate worst-case unlearning over various paraphrases and input formats. Our improved evaluation reveals that many unlearning methods are less effective than previously thought.
